beats.vo: Those seal videos all over your feed right now? Here's the thing nobody mentions. In America, touching one is a federal crime.
beats.cap:
TOUCHING A SEAL
IS A FEDERAL CRIME

beats.vo: In 1972, Congress passed the Marine Mammal Protection Act. It banned the take of any marine mammal — and take means harass, hunt, capture, or kill. Crowding a seal resting on the beach counts.

And people do get caught. One man got four years in prison under Hawaii law for repeatedly punching a pregnant monk seal — it's a felony there, and under federal law. A tourist who petted a resting seal and chased a sea turtle was caught by his own social media posts — a fifteen-hundred-dollar penalty. This year, federal agents arrested a man near Seattle accused of throwing a rock at a monk seal on Maui.

The law exists because of what came before it. In 1961 alone, an estimated half a million dolphins drowned in tuna nets — the fleet deliberately set on them. Hunters clubbed hundreds of thousands of harp seal pups on the ice every single year. Congress finally stepped in.

It worked — many species that were collapsing came back. But only about sixteen hundred Hawaiian monk seals are left. If you see one on the beach, stay fifty feet away — more if there's a pup. That's the line the feds draw. Cross it, and you're the one breaking federal law.
